messages.text.286f757d: If ‘young’ (少) is a quality still growing and unfolding, ‘old’ (老) is one that has fully ripened and reached a turning point. iYeok reads the change of old yin and old yang as a quality that deepens until the possibility of moving toward another quality opens up. Neither is better or higher than the other.

messages.text.7d0c79eb: We see the I Ching not as a tool for predicting the future, but as a guide for looking at who we are now and making life's choices. Interpretations are only a reference; the final judgment, and the responsibility for it, are your own. And in time, you should be able to look back on the choices you made.

Rather than a simple majority vote, iYeok also reads this as a question: “In this combination, which quality is given the deciding voice?”
messages.text.b82b82d4: We cannot choose the conditions we are born into, but there is no need to dislike the self we were born as. Nor do we need to confine ourselves to who we are now. What to accept and which direction to live in is ours to consider and choose. This is also why iYeok lets you choose among different methods.

messages.text.ca6075b5: Few (少) and many (多) refer to whether the number set aside in one round is small or large: 4 and 5 are small (few), 8 and 9 are large (many). The traditional method reads few as yang and many as yin. iYeok sees this pairing, too, not as a fixed answer but as a standard each person can choose, and plans to let you set it in the options. The details are in Learn's [Why did this line come out?].
messages.text.cd6e6b6f: We see yin and yang not as something divided by the body's sex, but as qualities that live in everyone. What we often call masculinity and femininity also live together in one person, and can show themselves in different ways through time, experience, and our own choices.

messages.text.ff63d4c3: Each trigram is made of three lines. When a lower trigram and an upper trigram meet, they form one of the 64 hexagrams.
messages.text.d69a1887: Just as you can choose how yin and yang are assigned to the lines, you can choose the order in which you view the eight trigrams.
messages.text.71be4605: The iYeok order counts yin as 0 and yang as 1 and reads the three lines from the top down as a binary number (000–111). It runs from the largest number down, with Qian (111) at the top and Kun (000) at the bottom. It keeps each trigram's unique number consistent with how iYeok stores and calculates, and follows the same rule as the 64-hexagram numbers.
messages.text.02cc5429: Changing the order doesn't change any trigram's lines or unique number. The choice also applies to [The eight trigrams] in yarrow and coin divination and to the ‘Trigram order’ setting.

messages.text.a2eb2fdb: Explore the eight trigrams — heaven, lake, fire, thunder, wind, water, mountain and earth — with pictures.
messages.text.4101e677: The Earlier Heaven order follows the Earlier Heaven numbering of the trigrams: Qian 1, Dui 2, Li 3, Zhen 4, Xun 5, Kan 6, Gen 7, Kun 8. It is different from the Later Heaven directional arrangement.
messages.text.61a33cb6: Note · Flip the binary number left to right
messages.text.590847bf: iYeok numbers put the top line on the left. If you flip the binary number left to right (for example, Dui 011₂ → 110₂), the Earlier Heaven order counts down one by one from 7 to 0. Read backwards from Kun, it runs from 0 to 7.
messages.text.2d5bb0d4: Qian 111 · Dui 110 · Li 101 · Zhen 100 · Xun 011 · Kan 010 · Gen 001 · Kun 000 (7 → 0)
messages.text.14bea37a: The order isn't the same as the iYeok order, but you can see it as the same binary numbers read from the other direction.
messages.text.22715418: Follow the two orders with the arrows on the arrangement above. Both start at heaven and end at earth. The numbers show each step.
messages.text.4ea88ece: The eight trigrams form pairs. Some pairs have opposite qualities, and some look alike.
messages.text.af1453d5: Flip yin and yang in all three lines (0 ↔ 1) and you get the trigram with the opposite quality. In numbers, it is 7 minus the value, so each pair always adds up to 7.
messages.text.2d84f76f: Heaven ↔ Earth and Water ↔ Fire: these four trigrams (Qian, Kun, Kan, Li) are the ones drawn on the Korean flag.
messages.text.962d8e5d: Similar pairs — only one line differs
messages.text.c0a99028: Trigrams that share the middle line and differ only in the top or bottom line can be seen as similar pairs. The differing line is shown in color.
messages.text.06a591bd: It's the same in the Earlier Heaven order and the iYeok order. Lay the eight trigrams out like beads on a string and fold it in the middle: the beads that touch are always opposite pairs.
messages.text.cb13c52b: In both orders the values count down from 7 to 0 (the Earlier Heaven order after flipping left to right), so facing positions always add up to 7.
messages.text.c1191081: Two ways to change a trigram
messages.text.074dd760: Flip yin and yang (0 ↔ 1): the quality becomes its opposite. Heaven ↔ Earth, Water ↔ Fire, Lake ↔ Mountain, Thunder ↔ Wind.
messages.text.f1e81786: Flip left to right (011₂ → 110₂): Lake ↔ Wind and Thunder ↔ Mountain swap, while Heaven, Earth, Water and Fire stay the same. The four that stay are the four on the Korean flag.
messages.text.0b8898a9: If you reverse how yin and yang are assigned to the lines, the same bar shapes read as the opposite trigrams. One choice turns the world the other way around.
messages.text.e0f80fb9: Write the trigrams as binary numbers and calculate line by line, and the answer is again one of the eight trigrams. Each calculation is a small change.
messages.text.4a8d6bfc: Line difference — how many lines differ
messages.text.04672f53: Count the lines that differ between two trigrams and you get how close or far apart they are. 1 means a similar pair, 3 means an opposite pair. Every trigram has three trigrams one line away, three two lines away and one three lines away.
messages.text.2827dfaf: Adding — 0 if the same, 1 if different
messages.text.73774fd6: Add place by place, 0 if the lines are the same and 1 if they differ, and you see which lines changed.
messages.text.638f5e7e: Adding Earth (000) changes nothing. Earth is “no change.”
messages.text.96ab775f: Adding Heaven (111) gives the opposite trigram.
messages.text.d52cc372: Adding a trigram to itself gives Earth (000), since nothing differs.
messages.text.56d2289b: The difference within a similar pair is Thunder (001, bottom line) or Mountain (100, top line); within an opposite pair it is Heaven (111).
messages.text.f0aab5c7: Adding the original and changed hexagrams this way shows where the changing lines are.
messages.text.1af682c7: Each place becomes 1 only when both lines are yang (1), so only the yang lines the two trigrams share remain.
messages.text.d8413a3b: Multiplying by Earth (000) turns anything into Earth.
messages.text.f8a19663: Multiplying an opposite pair always gives Earth (000), since they share no yang lines.
messages.text.e8aec886: In ordinary arithmetic, opposite pairs always add up to 7, and all eight values add up to 28.
messages.text.92895f99: Before the 64 hexagrams, let's look at the eight trigrams. Hold a figure in your hand and turn it, flip it, hold it up to a mirror: some trigrams change and some stay the same.
messages.text.f64a9960: Like black and white — same picture, different names
messages.text.6b9bab11: Draw three solid lines. Read solid as yang and it is Heaven (111); read it as yin and it is Earth (000). The picture hasn't changed at all — only the name has.
messages.text.7ff08f8d: Every opposite pair is the same picture read under the opposite convention. Like a black-and-white photo and its negative, they are as far apart and as opposite as can be, yet they can't be separated. So the eight trigrams are really four shapes, each with two faces.
messages.text.495a946e: Here are four ways of changing each of the eight trigrams. Faded cells are trigrams that stay the same.
messages.text.cdddabf2: Mirror (left ↔ right): each line looks the same both ways, so all eight trigrams stay the same.
messages.text.498aa363: Flip upside down (the same as turning 180°): Lake ↔ Wind and Thunder ↔ Mountain swap, while Heaven, Earth, Water and Fire stay the same. In binary it is the same as flipping left to right.
messages.text.303f1afa: Black ↔ white (yin ↔ yang): all eight trigrams turn into their opposites.
messages.text.3a5dd182: Flip and black ↔ white: Heaven ↔ Earth, Water ↔ Fire, Lake ↔ Thunder, Wind ↔ Mountain.
messages.text.97330067: Group the trigrams that can turn into one another by turning, flipping and swapping black and white, and the eight fall into three families.
messages.text.8f092141: Heaven · Earth: unchanged when flipped; swap black and white and each becomes the other.
messages.text.52918f14: Water · Fire: like Heaven and Earth — unchanged when flipped; swap black and white and each becomes the other.
messages.text.4a2edc4f: Lake · Wind · Mountain · Thunder: one family of four. Flip Lake and you get Wind, swap black and white and you get Mountain, do both and you get Thunder.
messages.text.7f5caeee: Heaven, Earth, Water and Fire — the ones that stay the same when flipped — are the four trigrams on the Korean flag.
messages.text.7d8038ae: With the 64 hexagrams the same thing happens across six lines. Eight hexagrams stay the same when flipped; the other 56 become different hexagrams.
messages.text.c66026cf: The distance between two trigrams is the number of lines that differ. There are only three steps — 1, 2 and 3 — and from any trigram there are three at distance 1, three at distance 2 and one at distance 3. Choose a center trigram.
messages.text.251a032c: Each change also moves a set distance: a mirror moves 0, a flip 0 or 2, black ↔ white always 3, and flip + black ↔ white 1 or 3.
messages.text.00956e0d: A short break — Qian, Kun, Kan, Li
messages.text.b7a8f360: Qian, Kun, Kan, Li — haven't you seen these somewhere? That's right: the Korean flag, Taegeukgi.
messages.text.4b8320b9: So let's draw it. Put the red and blue taegeuk in the middle, and Qian (Heaven), Kun (Earth), Kan (Water) and Li (Fire) in the four corners.
messages.text.befd3ad1: Top left Qian (Heaven) · bottom right Kun (Earth) · top right Kan (Water) · bottom left Li (Fire)
messages.text.bcc17bbd: The trigrams facing each other across the diagonals are opposite pairs (Qian ↔ Kun, Kan ↔ Li). As we saw above, these four stay the same when flipped upside down.
messages.text.37d73012: In the middle taegeuk, red (yang) above and blue (yin) below turn into each other — two dividing within one circle and becoming one again.
messages.text.5c8e32b6: The trigram lines are drawn from this page's trigram data. Proportions and colors follow the commonly cited specification, but haven't been checked against the official design file.
messages.text.2388cff9: And what happens if you turn the flag or flip it over?
messages.text.1200dde7: The flag as it is: Qian top left, Kun bottom right, Kan top right, Li bottom left.
messages.text.dd755947: Turn it 180° and Qian ↔ Kun and Kan ↔ Li swap places, and the red of the taegeuk goes to the bottom — as if heaven and earth had changed places.
messages.text.e11c59b1: Flip it upside down and Qian moves to Li's place and Kan to Kun's, while the red of the taegeuk goes to the bottom and the swirl turns the other way.
messages.text.7a893eb4: In a mirror, Qian moves to Kan's place and Li to Kun's; the red of the taegeuk stays on top, but the swirl turns the other way.
messages.text.945d8629: Either way, the shape of each of the four trigrams doesn't change, because Qian, Kun, Kan and Li stay the same however you turn or flip them. Only their places and the taegeuk change.
messages.text.d4051e82: Leave the flat page for 3D — turn the eight trigrams on a transparent octahedron with your own hands.
messages.text.51d1d731: The eight trigrams on an octahedron
messages.text.4ef1e490: Let's leave the flat page and go 3D. One trigram sits on each of the eight faces of a transparent regular octahedron. Turn it, zoom in, and tap a face to see its neighbors.
messages.text.b7a95512: A transparent regular octahedron with the eight trigrams on its faces
messages.text.51cffb33: Drag with one finger (or the mouse) to turn it, and pinch (or scroll) to zoom. Double-tap to return to the start. Tap a face to see its neighbors.
messages.text.21dc25d4: View from inside shows the octahedron as seen from within. It is the mirror image of the arrangement seen from outside.
messages.text.f97241e7: One line differs · neighbors sharing an edge
messages.text.b68f81eb: Two lines differ · faces touching only at a corner
messages.text.89a1ab24: Three lines differ · the parallel opposite face
messages.text.82e26d1c: All seven steps go to a face sharing an edge — a path through all eight trigrams changing one line at a time.
messages.text.0fb46813: Dashed steps jump to a face that isn't a neighbor. An order strung in a line on the flat page breaks up here and there on the octahedron.
messages.text.174885c8: The rule of this octahedron — lines = axes
messages.text.dddf442a: The top line takes up–down, the middle line front–back, and the bottom line left–right. Yang puts a trigram on one side of that axis, yin on the other. The four upper faces hold Qian, Xun, Gen and Li (top line yang); the four lower faces hold Dui, Kan, Kun and Zhen.
messages.text.e659b3a2: Faces sharing an edge always differ by one line (all 12 pairs).
messages.text.902b6bcd: Faces touching only at a corner differ by two lines; parallel opposite faces differ by three — the opposite pairs (all 4 pairs).
messages.text.2d658a2f: The four faces meeting at a corner share one line. Six corners = three lines × yin and yang.
messages.text.e6372970: From any face: three neighbors, three corner-touching faces, one opposite — the same as the three steps of distance between trigrams.
messages.text.adc863ce: The calculations and changes from the trigram page become ways of moving the solid.
messages.text.d845de4d: Through the center to the opposite face (point reflection)
messages.text.342922b2: Adding Zhen, Kan or Gen (one yang line)
messages.text.ecb1f7e6: Adding Dui, Li or Xun (two yang lines)
messages.text.2111a366: Flipping upside down (swapping top and bottom lines)
messages.text.ba485bc0: Follow the Earlier Heaven or iYeok order across the faces and three of the seven steps have to jump to a face that isn't a neighbor. Try it with [Follow a path] above.
messages.text.037029b3: Multiplying isn't a movement. It folds things toward the yin side, so several faces collapse onto one.
messages.text.c3d2f14b: With the same eight faces, the rules change depending on how you place the trigrams. There are 40,320 ways to put eight trigrams on eight faces, or 1,680 if you count arrangements that match after turning the solid as one.
messages.text.cf2c7e4c: Only opposite pairs facing each other
messages.text.0698de7d: Earlier Heaven order, upper four then lower four
messages.text.2f3a9c66: iYeok order, upper four then lower four
messages.text.24436186: There are 48 'lines = axes' arrangements, but turned around they are all one shape and its mirror image. Seen from inside the transparent octahedron, it is exactly that mirror image.
messages.text.03da8ab3: There are 384 ways to put only the opposite pairs facing each other (16 after turning), and only 2 of them are 'lines = axes'. The rest get the opposites right but some neighbors differ by two lines — half tangled.
messages.text.eccb776b: Cut five edges and lay the octahedron flat to get a net. There are 384 ways to cut it, or 11 shapes after turning and flipping.
messages.text.f22b9733: Every time you cross a fold line, exactly one line changes. A net is a map of one-line changes.
messages.text.2ecfaee4: Three of the 11 are a single unbranched strip. The picture below is one of them — the [One line at a time] path above, unfolded.
messages.text.b8f45281: The triangles, which alternate in direction, split exactly by whether the number of yang lines is odd or even. Dark cells are Qian, Zhen, Kan and Gen (odd); light cells are Kun, Xun, Li and Dui (even).
messages.text.96272a54: Opposite pairs differ in all three lines, so in a net they never share an edge, and one is always dark and the other light.
messages.text.208c5f62: The net of the one-line-at-a-time path
messages.text.3568ecaa: Tradition also calls Qian the father, Zhen, Kan and Gen the three sons, Kun the mother, and Xun, Li and Dui the three daughters. That matches the odd/even split exactly, though these names are given here without checking the original texts.
messages.text.4cfeb89f: All the counts on this page (40,320 · 1,680 · 48 · 384 · 16 · 11 · 3) were checked by direct calculation.
messages.text.28937806: Part 2 — beads this time. Eight beads tied with rubber bands draw together in the cold and sulk in the heat.
messages.text.3446f239: iYeok · Explore the trigrams further, part 2
messages.text.813a8055: Eight beads that push and pull, face each other and sulk
messages.text.a2a41e10: Eight trigram beads sit in eight directions at the same distance from the center of a sphere, and beads one line apart are tied with rubber bands. Change the temperature and opposite beads pull together or push apart like magnets. Turn it around and watch what happens to the other beads and the bands.
messages.text.8734f48a: Eight trigram beads tied with rubber bands
messages.text.393f00d4: Drag with one finger (or the mouse) to turn, pinch (or scroll) to zoom, and double-tap to return to the starting view. Tap two beads to see their distance and line difference.
messages.text.85da91c7: At normal temperature there's no magnetic pull, so the beads stay in the original cube, turning round and round in place.
messages.text.7bd9f2be: In the cold, the chosen pair turn to face each other and meet in the middle. The other six beads stay put: rubber bands can't push, so only the six bands tied to that pair go slack.
messages.text.e688038a: In the heat, the chosen pair turn their backs and move apart. The stretched bands pull the other six beads in toward the axis, and the whole thing becomes a long spindle.
messages.text.ce0d5265: When all four pairs pull together, every bead faces its pair and the eight crowd into a small cube of touching beads. All the bands go slack.
messages.text.47e1162b: When all four pairs push apart, every bead turns its back on its pair, and the cube swells while keeping its shape. All the bands stretch evenly.
messages.text.749329e4: Tap a bead. Tap two to compare their distance and line difference.
messages.text.9218eefc: The rules of the beads and bands
messages.text.53e3effa: The beads sit at the corners of a cube, using the same 'lines = axes' rule as the octahedron page: the top line is up–down, the middle front–back, the bottom left–right. It's the octahedron with a bead set in the middle of each face and the faces taken away.
messages.text.c6e2584f: In the starting position, the actual distance between beads is the line difference.
messages.text.c4208cb9: Squared, the distances are exactly proportional to the line difference (1 : 2 : 3).
messages.text.0c3b0e19: Here's what happens when the opposite pairs become magnets. Try it in the picture above.
messages.text.b4020c91: Only that pair's six go slack
messages.text.69d36fe6: When one pair pulls together, the others don't budge because rubber bands only pull and never push. When one pair moves apart, the bands that tie everything together make the whole shape follow.
messages.text.dd003d4c: Normal: turning round and round in place
messages.text.3816abd0: Hot: turning its back on its opposite (sulking)
messages.text.0963b5e9: When the face (the trigram) looks toward us it's clear; turned sideways it narrows; turned away it fades.
messages.text.f885b3fc: This is a simple physical model: bands pull only when stretched, the magnetic force is constant at any distance, and beads bounce off each other. The direction of the faces shows mood and isn't part of the position calculation.
messages.text.d496725f: This time the rubber bands become magic staffs. A staff can both pull and push, and it grows or shrinks at a word. Pick staffs and stretch or shrink them as you like.
messages.text.af244b85: Eight trigram beads joined by twelve magic staffs
messages.text.8aca705a: Tap a staff in the picture or choose it with the buttons below. Turning and zooming work as above.
messages.text.343b96bb: Stretch the four staffs of one line together and you get a box stretched only in that line's direction. Only beads that differ in that line move apart; everything else stays.
messages.text.c6d7ba65: Stretch or shrink just one staff and the others keep their length (0% strain on the other staffs). Instead, the box twists and leans: a cube frame made only of edges isn't rigid, so it can change shape while every staff keeps its length.
messages.text.60a1303e: Unlike rubber bands, staffs can push: shrinking one pulls its two beads together, stretching it pushes them apart.
messages.text.da972515: Take the opposite-pair staffs out and change just one staff: the others keep their length (0% strain on the other staffs), and the box twists and leans instead. A cube frame made only of edges isn't rigid, so it can change shape while every staff keeps its length.
messages.text.042ee6f6: Put the four opposite-pair staffs in and the frame becomes rigid. Now changing just one staff makes all the others stretch and shrink a little to hold it (the strain rises above 0%). The opposite pairs running through the center hold the whole thing together.
messages.text.fad373c2: Stretch all four opposite-pair staffs together and the cube tries to grow while keeping its shape, with the edge staffs pulling back.
messages.text.da85fbe3: The opposite pair met in the middle — like the Herdsman and the Weaver Girl!
messages.text.5e887eeb: Shrink an opposite-pair staff to ×0.2 and the two beads touch in the middle. The length scale has the original length (×1) in the center, with ×0.2 on the left and ×5 on the right the same factor away.
messages.text.5260896d: The board is the eight beads stretched out in counting order. Throw three coins and race between Earth (Kun) and Heaven (Qian). The number of spaces between trigrams follows the distances between the eight beads.
messages.text.c05c2579: These are first-draft rules — we'll fix them as we play.
messages.text.090c9ea7: Reach the end in as few throws as you can
messages.text.70733c5d: The computer throws on its own
messages.text.f1a2b2d6: Capturing: land on the other piece to send it back to its start

messages.text.e8cb79ac: Both players start from a Human (人) bead. The winner of rock, paper, scissors picks the Earth (Kun) or Heaven (Qian) side and throws first. The first to reach the trigram at the far end wins.
messages.text.4b40916f: Stop exactly on a trigram and you throw again. Old yang or old yin sends you to the opposite trigram — its mirror spot across the middle of the board. Before the middle that's a lucky leap; past the middle it can ruin you.
messages.text.0ffcc71a: No further extra throw after a jump or an extra throw. You can't go back past your start, and going past the goal counts as arriving.
messages.text.6a0757d8: Heads count 3 and tails 2 (sum 7 young yang, 8 young yin, 9 old yang, 6 old yin). Young yang and young yin each come up 3/8 of the time; old yang and old yin each 1/8.
messages.text.5461befb: Can't go back past the start.
messages.text.a707de52: Level 1: a board game racing between Earth and Heaven with three coins
messages.text.be0035f5: Both players start from a Human (人) bead: the Heaven (Qian) side's at the very top of the board, the Earth (Kun) side's at the very bottom. The winner of rock, paper, scissors picks a side and throws first. Pass the trigram at the far end and reach the Human bead beyond it first to win — the finish is a person, not a trigram.
messages.text.5fcc0071: From the top Human bead, Heaven (Qian) side
messages.text.2dda427c: From the bottom Human bead, Earth (Kun) side
messages.text.0380073b: No further extra throw after a jump or an extra throw; the turn passes to the other player. You can't go back past your start.
messages.text.5e2b6ac5: You must land exactly on the Human bead at the end. If the roll is too big, you go up to it and bounce back by the extra spaces. For example, a young yin on the last trigram (Kun or Qian) takes you to the Human bead and back to that trigram, so you throw once more: young yang wins, old yang or old yin jumps to the opposite trigram, and young yin leaves you there and passes the turn.
messages.text.1fdd3c6a: Exactly on the Human bead! Bounce back by the extra spaces.
messages.text.cbb92b76: Playing solo — no one to push.
messages.text.f9fe28ef: Stop exactly on a trigram and you throw again. Old yang sends you to the opposite trigram — its mirror spot across the middle of the board. Before the middle that's a lucky leap; past the middle it can ruin you. Old yin pushes the other player's piece back 3 spaces instead of yours (never past their start).
messages.text.a197af18: You must land exactly on the Human bead at the end. If the roll is too big, you go up to it and bounce back by the extra spaces. For example, a young yin on the last trigram (Kun or Qian) takes you to the Human bead and back to that trigram, so you throw once more: young yang wins, old yang jumps to the opposite trigram, old yin pushes the other piece back 3, and young yin leaves you there and passes the turn.

messages.text.8445a38a: One side of each coin is yang, the other yin. Among the three coins, the side that appears only once gives the name: one yang is young yang, one yin is young yin. If all three match, the result is old: all yang is old yang, all yin is old yin. Young means a force still growing; old means a force that has reached its fullest and is ready to turn into its opposite, so in this game old yang and old yin shake up the board with jumps and pushes. Young yang and young yin each come up 3/8 of the time, old yang and old yin 1/8 each.
messages.text.534d0c93: Both players start from a Human (人) bead: the Heaven (Qian) side's at the very top of the board, the Earth (Kun) side's at the very bottom. Player 1 (you, when playing the computer) picks a side and throws first. Pass the trigram at the far end and reach the Human bead beyond it first to win — the finish is a person, not a trigram.
messages.text.9637f5cd: two bands of 8 trigram beads, joined
messages.text.dc14add1: Two levels means two bands of 8 trigram beads joined end to end. After Qian on the first band comes Kun on the second (all three lines differ, so the gap is the √3 distance), and the Human beads stay at both ends. On two levels the extra-throw rule changes: old yang jumps to the opposite trigram on the other level, old yin to the opposite trigram on the same level (no pushing the other piece).
messages.text.9383c37e: Jump to the opposite trigram on the other level!
messages.text.5a328f6f: Jump to the opposite trigram on the same level!
messages.text.19e1e39b: With the reversed rule, young yang and young yin swap their moves: young yin goes 1 space and young yang 2 (on both normal and extra throws). Old yang and old yin stay the same. The table above shows the iYeok rule.
